english: The most important thing is first to show that the differential equation has no critical points other than $z = 0, 1, \infty$.
topic: The page identifies certain recursively defined expressions with the Sturm functions (the last being the discriminant) and then sets up the continued-fraction expansion of $(1-z)^\alpha$ via a second-order linear differential equation for an auxiliary function.

triage.modern_statement: For the continued-fraction (Padé-type) expansion of the binomial function (1-z)^α, Hilbert introduces an auxiliary function, built from the convergents or remainders. It satisfies a second-order linear ODE with rational coefficients. The step he leaves open is to show that this ODE is Fuchsian with singular points only at z = 0, 1 and ∞. If so, it is a Riemann P-equation, so it reduces to Gauss's hypergeometric equation. The convergent denominators and remainders are then 2F1 / Jacobi-type functions, and their convergence can be read off from the known behaviour of hypergeometric functions. This is a lemma inside a classical theory, not a stand-alone research problem.
triage.answered_by: No source found that answers Hilbert's note directly. The surrounding theory was classical before or around his time. Gauss gave continued fractions for ratios of hypergeometric series, which include (1-z)^α as 2F1(-α,b;b;z). Riemann's posthumous fragment (1863) treated these via the hypergeometric differential equation. Laguerre (J. Math. Pures Appl. 1885) studied continued fractions of functions that satisfy a first-order linear ODE with rational coefficients, a class containing (1-z)^α. Padé (Ann. ENS 1907) proved convergence for continued-fraction expansions of a related class of functions. Today it is standard that Padé approximants of 2F1(a,1;c;z), including binomial-type functions, are expressed through hypergeometric functions and polynomials.

evidence.claim: Gauss's continued fraction is a classical family of continued fractions built from hypergeometric functions. This is the framework in which (1-z)^α = 2F1(-α,·;·;z) is expanded.

Laguerre, 'Sur la réduction en fractions continues d'une fraction qui satisfait à une équation différentielle linéaire du premier ordre dont les coefficients sont rationnels', J. Math. Pures Appl. (4) 1 (1885), 135–165. This is the general theory covering (1-z)^α, where the convergents satisfy linear ODEs.
Later work continued Laguerre's result on continued-fraction solutions of first-order linear ODEs.
Padé, 'Recherches sur la convergence des développements en fractions continues d'une certaine catégorie de fonctions', Ann. Sci. ENS (3) 24 (1907), 341–400.
Modern work on convergence of ray sequences of Padé approximants to 2F1(a,1;c;z) shows that the Padé table of these hypergeometric functions is explicitly understood.

triage.why: The note is a step in a proof: showing that an auxiliary second-order ODE has only the singular points 0, 1 and ∞, which makes it hypergeometric. Gauss, Riemann, Laguerre and Padé had already developed continued fractions for (1-z)^α and other hypergeometric quotients, and this kind of fact is standard there. The explicit hypergeometric form of the Padé approximants of 2F1 is textbook material. I found no source that discusses Hilbert's particular auxiliary function. So 'solved' means 'settled within known classical theory', not that someone answered this note specifically. The note is not among Hilbert's 23 problems or the 24th problem. Confidence is medium because I cannot see the exact definition of the auxiliary function on the page.
